draft.title: Links between rural and urban places
card: Rural and urban places depend on each other. Goods, money, people and services flow between them.
Cities rely on rural areas for food, water and energy. For example, farms near Sydney and further inland supply produce, and dams in rural catchments store much of the city's water.
Rural areas rely on cities as markets for what they produce. They also use city services such as specialist hospitals, universities, banks and airports.
Because the flows go both ways, a change in one place can affect the other. A drought on farms can raise food prices in cities. A fall in city demand can cut farm incomes.
draft.remember: Cities draw food, water and energy from rural areas. Rural areas draw markets and services from cities.

a.q: Which statement best describes the link between a city and its rural surroundings?
opts: Each relies on the other for things it cannot supply itself
Cities supply all goods and rural areas only supply land
Rural areas supply everything and cities supply nothing
The two are separate and do not affect each other
a.why: Cities need rural food, water and energy, while rural areas need city markets and services, so the dependence runs both ways. The option saying rural areas only supply land is tempting, but the card shows rural areas supply food, water and energy.
a.clue: Think about which way the flows go.

b.q: A long drought cuts wheat harvests on farms around Dubbo. Which effect on city places is most likely to follow?
opts: Higher food prices in cities that buy the wheat products
Lower food prices because cities grow their own wheat
No change, because cities do not depend on farms
Farm incomes rise because cities buy more wheat
b.why: Cities depend on rural areas for food, so a smaller harvest can push up food prices there. The option saying farm incomes rise reverses cause and effect: less produce to sell does not raise demand from city markets.
b.clue: Cities rely on farms for food supply.

a.best: Each relies on the other for things it cannot supply itself

b.best: Higher food prices in cities that buy the wheat products

problems.detail: Too easy for Year 12 HSC. Three distractors are absolute or absurd ('separate and do not affect each other', 'supply everything and cities supply nothing', 'cities supply all goods'), so the right option can be picked without knowing the idea.

Why (b) says the 'farm incomes rise' option 'reverses cause and effect', which is not an accurate description. That option is wrong because a smaller harvest means less to sell, and because it describes farms, not the city effect the question asks about.

check.summary: The card is accurate and both intended answers are correct. Question a is far too easy for Year 12 because its distractors are absurd, and the why for b describes the farm-income distractor confusingly.

proposal.title: Links between rural and urban places
card: Rural and urban places depend on each other. Goods, money, people and services flow between them.

a.q: Which example shows a rural place relying on a city for a service?
opts: A Dubbo farmer travels to Sydney for specialist cancer care
Sydney draws drinking water from a dam in a rural catchment
A farmer uses the bank branch in their own small town
A Sydney family pays for a weekend stay on a rural farm
a.why: The farmer is leaving a rural area to use a specialist hospital in the city, which is a rural need for a city service. Sydney's water from a rural dam is a real link, but it runs the other way: the city relies on the rural area. The bank in the farmer's own town is a rural service, not a city one.
a.clue: Check where the person lives and where the service is.

b.q: A long drought cuts wheat harvests on farms around Dubbo. Which effect on city places is most likely to follow?
opts: Higher food prices in cities that buy the wheat products
Lower food prices because cities grow their own wheat
No change, because cities do not depend on farms
Farm incomes rise because cities buy more wheat
b.why: Cities depend on rural areas for food, so a smaller harvest can push up food prices there. The option saying farm incomes rise is wrong because a smaller harvest leaves farms with less wheat to sell, and it describes an effect on farms, not the city effect the question asks about.
b.clue: Cities rely on farms for food supply.

a.best: A Dubbo farmer travels to Sydney for specialist cancer care

b.best: Higher food prices in cities that buy the wheat products

problems.detail: The distractors are implausible for Year 12: 'cities do not depend on farms' and 'cities grow their own wheat' are absurd, and the clue restates the answer. A student can answer without understanding the two-way flow.

Australian wheat prices are largely set by export and world markets, so a drought confined to farms around Dubbo would have little effect on city food prices. A widespread drought, or a fresh-produce example, would fit the card's claim better.

check.summary: The card and Question a are sound. Question b is too easy for Year 12 because of weak distractors and a clue that restates the answer, and a local wheat drought is a shaky example of city food prices rising.
